344.title: The prayer at the foundations
344.hook: Ibrahim and Isma'il pray for a messenger from among the people (2:127–129)
344.carry: pray for the ones not born
344.tomorrow: What will you worship after me
344.howItsDone: Muslims often recite Ibrahim and Isma'il's words, Rabbana taqabbal minna, our Lord, accept from us, after completing a good deed, and pray for their children and for generations to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim tested, and your line, tested, then trusted. Today, Ibrahim again, with stones in his hands.

Old buildings sometimes have a time capsule sealed into a cornerstone: a newspaper, a few coins, a letter to whoever opens it in a hundred years. The builders will never meet that reader. They write anyway. In al-Baqarah, a father and son are raising the foundations of a house in a dry valley in Arabia. As they lift the stones, they speak, and much of what they say is for people who don't exist yet. Today: the prayer at the foundations.
screen: `A LETTER IN THE CORNERSTONE.` → `A FATHER AND SON, LIFTING STONES.` → `WORDS FOR PEOPLE NOT YET BORN.`

segments.voice: Last year you watched Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the Kaaba. This year, listen to what they said while they did it. Verse one hundred twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.” They're building God's house, and their first words ask that it be accepted, as if it might not be. Then the prayer grows. Make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a nation submissive to You. Show us our rites, and turn to us. Then, in verse one hundred twenty-nine, the furthest request: Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves, who will recite Your verses to them, teach them the book and wisdom, and purify them. Muslims hold that it was answered long after, in the same valley, in Mecca, with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has him say: I am the answer to the prayer of my father Ibrahim, and the good news of Isa. Notice the order inside the prayer. Accept what we did. Make us good. Make our children good. Send them a teacher. It moves outward, from the two of them to people they'd never see. The stones they lifted can't be pointed to today. The prayer is still read, in this surah, every day.
screen: `OUR LORD! ACCEPT FROM US` · `FROM US, TO OUR DESCENDANTS` · `A MESSENGER FROM AMONG THEM` · `I AM THE ANSWER TO IBRAHIM'S PRAYER`

segments.voice: Hold in mind people you'll never meet, or barely will: grandchildren, your students' students, whoever lives in your home after you, a child born this year far away. If you pray, use the builders' first words, Our Lord, accept from us, and then ask good for them in your own words; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Kaaba. The house Ibrahim and Isma'il raised in Mecca, praying as they built it for descendants and a messenger not yet born. Today's word.
Your line: pray for the ones not born. The builders at the Kaaba did. See you tomorrow.

345.title: What will you worship after me
345.hook: the dying Ya'qub asks his sons, and they answer, your God and the God of your fathers (2:133)
345.carry: what will you keep after me
345.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to prepare a wasiyyah, a will, and some add words of counsel for their families about faith and conduct, following the example of Ibrahim and Ya'qub in al-Baqarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the prayer at the foundations, and your line, pray for the ones not born. Ibrahim prayed for his descendants. Today, two generations on, one of them is dying.

At a bedside near the end, the last conversations tend to be short, and about what matters. The mortgage doesn't come up. They ask: are you going to be all right? Will you look after your sister? Do you remember what I taught you? Al-Baqarah takes us into a room like that: an old man, his sons gathered around the bed, and one question. Today: what will you worship after me.
screen: `THE LAST CONVERSATIONS ARE SHORT.` → `AN OLD MAN, HIS SONS AROUND THE BED.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The old man is Ya'qub, Ibrahim's grandson, also called Israel. The verse before says Ibrahim had given his sons a charge, and Ya'qub did the same: God has chosen the religion for you, so don't die except in submission to Him. Then verse one hundred thirty-three asks the listener directly: were you there when death came to Ya'qub? And it lets us in. He says to his sons, in Pickthall's words: “What will ye worship after me?” Not what will you do with the flocks, not who gets what. The one thing he wants to know before he goes. They answer with a chain of names: we will worship your God, the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we submit. Notice one name. Isma'il isn't Ya'qub's father; he's his uncle, the brother of his father Ishaq. The commentators point out that Arabic can count an uncle among the fathers. The sons name both branches of the family in one breath, as one line of faith. In Islamic tradition, a deathbed charge like this has a name: wasiyyah, a counsel, a will. Muslims are encouraged to write a will for their property, and some also leave words for their families about prayer, kindness and keeping ties. Ya'qub's charge was already given. At the very end, he doesn't repeat it. He asks, and lets his sons say it in their own voices.
screen: `WERE YOU THERE WHEN DEATH CAME?` · `WHAT WILL YE WORSHIP AFTER ME?` · `A CHAIN OF NAMES, BOTH BRANCHES` · `WASIYYAH: THE LAST COUNSEL`

segments.voice: Think of someone who will carry something of you after you, a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend, and ask what one thing you hope they keep: not a possession, but a habit, a way of treating people, a word, a faith. Put it into one plain sentence and hold it quietly.
Wasiyyah. A last counsel, a will — Ya'qub's deathbed charge to his sons, asking what they would worship after him. Today's word.
Your line: what will you keep after me. Ya'qub let his sons answer in their own words. Day three hundred forty-five, done.

346.title: A middle people
346.hook: We made you a community of the middle way (2:143)
346.howItsDone: Muslim scholars often cite 2:143 and the hadith of the three men in Bukhari when teaching moderation in worship: steady, sustainable practice rather than extremes of devotion or neglect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ya'qub's wasiyyah, and your line, what will you keep after me. Today, a word about a whole community.

Al-Baqarah has two hundred eighty-six verses. Divide by two, and you land on verse one hundred forty-three. Many readers have noticed that the verse in the middle of the longest surah is the verse about being in the middle. Whether that's design or coincidence, the Qur'an doesn't say, and scholars don't build anything on it. But it makes the verse easy to find, and it fits what the verse says. Today: wasat.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED EIGHTY-SIX, DIVIDED BY TWO.` → `VERSE ONE HUNDRED FORTY-THREE.` → `THE MIDDLE VERSE, ABOUT THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Last year you met this verse in the story of the qiblah turning toward Mecca. This year, look at one word. In Pickthall's words: “Thus We have appointed you a middle nation.” The Arabic is ummatan wasatan. Wasat means the middle, the center, but in Arabic the middle is also the best part: the middle of the valley, where the water runs; the middle of the family, the most honored. A hadith in Bukhari explains the word in this very verse with one other: 'adl, just, balanced. The verse gives a reason: a middle people, so that you may be witnesses over humanity, and the messenger a witness over you. A witness has to stand where both sides can be seen; you can't see the whole field from one end zone. So what does the middle look like in a life? Bukhari tells of three men who asked about the Prophet's worship and found it less than they expected. One said: I'll pray all night, every night. Another: I'll fast every day. A third: I'll never marry. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to them and said, in effect: I'm the most mindful of God among you, and I fast and I eat, I pray and I sleep, and I marry. Whoever turns from my way is not of me. The middle isn't lukewarm. It's the balance that lets someone keep going for a lifetime, and see both sides clearly enough to be a fair witness.
screen: `UMMATAN WASATAN: A MIDDLE NATION` · `THE MIDDLE IS THE BEST PART` · `A WITNESS STANDS WHERE BOTH SIDES SHOW` · `I FAST AND I EAT, I PRAY AND I SLEEP`

segments.voice: Look for one place in your life that has drifted to an end: working every evening, scrolling past midnight, swearing off sugar forever, or doing nothing at all for something you care about. Picture its middle, not zero and not everything, the amount you could keep up for a year, and rest there for a few breaths.

347.title: Remember Me
347.hook: remember Me, I will remember you, be grateful and don't deny (2:152)
347.howItsDone: Muslims practice dhikr, repeating short phrases such as subhan Allah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar after prayer and through the day, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wasat, and your line, the middle way. Today, a verse a few lines after the middle, that begins with the word therefore.

Some promises take a long time to arrive. A grandmother saves for a grandchild's education, and the grandchild graduates years after she's gone. A letter mailed long ago turns up in the right hands at last. Three days ago, Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed for a messenger who would come long after them. Today al-Baqarah reaches back to that prayer, says it's been answered, and asks one thing in return. Today: remember Me.
screen: `A PROMISE THAT TAKES A LONG TIME.` → `THE PRAYER AT THE FOUNDATIONS.` → `ANSWERED, AND ONE THING ASKED.`

segments.voice: Put two verses side by side. Verse one hundred twenty-nine, Ibrahim's prayer: send them a messenger from among them, who will recite Your verses, teach the book and wisdom, and purify them. Verse one hundred fifty-one, God speaking to the first Muslims: We have sent among you a messenger from among you, who recites Our verses to you, purifies you, teaches you the book and wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know. Everything Ibrahim asked for, and one thing more, twenty-two verses apart. Commentators notice the order changes too: in the answer, purifying comes before teaching. Then the very next verse, in Pickthall's words: “Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.” Therefore: because the prayer was answered, because the gift arrived. Al-Baqarah doesn't ask for payment. It asks for remembrance, and then for gratitude: give thanks to Me, and don't deny Me. Remembrance and gratitude side by side, like one act seen from two angles. And it's a two-way promise: you remember; you are remembered. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari adds one detail: whoever remembers God in a gathering, God remembers them in a better gathering. Last year you learned dhikr, the practice of remembering. Here the Qur'an puts it right after a gift long in coming. The community was remembered first, in a prayer said over stones long before. It remembers back, and is remembered back.
screen: `THE PRAYER (2:129), THE ANSWER (2:151)` · `THEREFORE REMEMBER ME` · `REMEMBRANCE AND GRATITUDE, SIDE BY SIDE` · `REMEMBERED FIRST, REMEMBERED BACK`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one short phrase you know, subhan Allah, alhamdulillah or Allahu akbar, and say it softly with the breath, counting on your fingers if you like. If you don't, bring back one person who remembered you when you needed it, and let their name return with each breath, unhurried.

348.title: To Him we return
348.hook: those who, struck by loss, say we belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156)
348.carry: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
348.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or any misfortune, and many add the supplication taught in Sahih Muslim asking God for reward in the loss and something better in its place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: remember Me, and your line, remembered back. Today the surah keeps reading, and the next thing it promises is a test.

A phone buzzes in a family group chat: someone's uncle has died. Within minutes the replies stack up, and if the family is Muslim, many are the same short Arabic line, typed in full or just the letters. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Even people with little Arabic often know it. It's said at funerals, on hearing bad news, even when a phone screen cracks. It comes from al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six. Today: to Him we return.
screen: `A MESSAGE IN THE FAMILY CHAT.` → `THE SAME SHORT LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `AL-BAQARAH, VERSE 156.`

segments.voice: Read the line where it sits. Just after remember Me comes a warning, not a comfort: God will surely test people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and harvests. Then: give good news to the patient, those who, when a calamity strikes them, say, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” Two halves. We belong to God: whatever was lost was never fully ours, and neither are we. And to Him we return: the loss isn't the end of the road. The next verse says on such people are blessings from their Lord, and mercy, and they are the rightly guided. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows what this did in one life. Umm Salamah heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by a loss and says these words, adding, O God, reward me in my loss and give me something better in its place, will be given something better. Then her husband, Abu Salamah, died. She said the words, and wondered: who could be better than Abu Salamah, the first family to emigrate? She said them anyway. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. In the hadith, she is the one telling the story. And the line is spoken in the plural: we belong, we return. Even someone grieving alone says it as part of a we, which may be why it fits a family chat so well.
screen: `FIRST, A PROMISED TEST` · `WE BELONG TO GOD; WE RETURN TO HIM` · `UMM SALAMAH SAID IT ANYWAY` · `SPOKEN IN THE PLURAL`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one loss, recent or old, large or small, and let yourself feel it for a moment without pushing it away. Then, if you're Muslim or wish to, say the line slowly, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un; if not, hold its two halves in English: this was never fully mine, and this isn't the end of the road.

Your line: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. We belong to God, and to Him we return. Go gently.

349.title: Signs for those who think
349.hook: ships on the sea, rain, winds, clouds between sky and earth (2:164)
349.howItsDone: Muslims call both the verses of the Qur'an and the features of the natural world ayat, signs, and teachers encourage reflection, tafakkur, on rain, sky and creatures as a form of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Salamah, and your line, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Today al-Baqarah lifts its eyes from loss to the sky.

A cargo ship, longer than a city block, slides into a harbor carrying the bananas you'll buy next week. Over it, a weather front rolls in from the sea: a gray wall of cloud, water hanging in the air, held up by nothing you can see. Then the wind turns, rain falls on the hills behind the town, and soon the hills are green. Ordinary things, seen so often they're barely seen. Al-Baqarah asks for another look. Today: signs for those who think.
screen: `A CARGO SHIP SLIDES INTO HARBOR.` → `WATER HANGING IN THE AIR.` → `LOOK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred sixty-four is a list. Count with me. The creation of the heavens and the earth. The alternation of night and day. Ships that run on the sea with what benefits people. The water God sends down from the sky, bringing the earth to life after it was dead. Every kind of creature scattered across it. The turning of the winds. And the clouds, held in service between sky and earth. Seven things, and then: in these are signs for people who use their reason. Two words carry the verse. The first is ayat, signs, the same word Muslims use for the verses of the Qur'an. A line of the book is an ayah, and so is a cloud; the book and the world are both read. The second is ya'qilun, those who reason. It comes from 'aql, the mind, and the classical dictionaries connect that root to 'iqal, the cord used to tie a camel so it doesn't wander off. To reason, in that picture, is to hold a thought still long enough to follow it. Other verses end with a similar call: for those who think, who reflect, who understand. Faith, here, isn't asked to look away from the world. It's asked to look harder at it. Some Muslim scholars, astronomers and physicians among them, pointed to verses like this as a reason to study.
screen: `SEVEN THINGS, COUNTED` · `AYAH: A VERSE, AND A CLOUD` · `'AQL: TO HOLD A THOUGHT STILL` · `LOOK HARDER AT THE WORLD`

segments.voice: Find a cloud, through a window or outside, and stay with it: watch its edge change, which way it moves, and how fast. If there are no clouds, watch whatever moves, a tree in the wind, light on a wall, without naming or explaining it, the way you'd read a line slowly.
Ayah. A sign — the same word Muslims use for a verse of the Qur'an, given here to ships, rain, winds and clouds. Today's word.

350.title: Not east or west
350.hook: righteousness is not turning your face east or west, but belief, giving, keeping promises, patience (2:177)
350.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 2:177 as a summary of faith in practice: belief together with charity, prayer, zakat, keeping promises and patience; the same word, birr, names kindness to parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ayah, a sign, and your line, look harder at the world. Today, the end of a week, and a verse that looks at people the way yesterday's looked at clouds.

A few pages back, al-Baqarah told of the qiblah turning: the direction of prayer moved from Jerusalem to Mecca, and some people argued about it loudly. Which way is right? Which way is holy? An argument about a direction can run a long time without anyone having to change how they live. Further on in the same surah, one verse steps over the whole argument with a single sentence. Today: birr.
screen: `THE QIBLAH TURNED.` → `WHICH WAY IS RIGHT?` → `ONE SENTENCE STEPS OVER IT.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred seventy-seven, in Pickthall's words: “It is not righteousness that ye turn your faces to the East and the West.” The word is birr: righteousness, goodness, devotion, the same word Muslims use for kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn. Then the verse says what birr is, in a long, concrete list. Belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the book, the prophets. Giving wealth, though you love it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and to free those in bondage. Establishing the prayer and paying the zakat. Keeping your promises when you make them. And patience in poverty, in sickness, and in the moment of danger. Commentators read one phrase two ways: giving wealth 'ala hubbihi can mean despite loving it, or out of love for God. Both readings have their teachers. The verse doesn't say direction doesn't matter; Muslims still face the Kaaba when they pray. It says facing the right way isn't, by itself, goodness. Goodness is belief that shows up as giving, praying, keeping your word, and holding steady when things go wrong. Look back at the week: builders who prayed for people not yet born, a father asking what his sons would keep, a middle people, remembrance, loss, the clouds. Each day was a piece of this one list.
screen: `NOT EAST, NOT WEST` · `BIRR: GOODNESS, DEVOTION` · `BELIEF, GIVING, PROMISES, PATIENCE` · `THE WEEK, IN ONE LIST`

segments.voice: Think back over the last week to what you said you'd do: call back, send the file, fix the shelf, visit, pay someone back. Find one you haven't kept yet, and picture keeping it in the plainest way, holding the decision quietly, like something already done.
Birr. Righteousness, goodness, devotion. Al-Baqarah says it's not facing east or west, but belief, giving, prayer, keeping promises, and patience. Today's word.
Your line: righteousness is what you do. Small promises count too. Three hundred fifty days, and counting.
